title: Data Types & Numerical Precision 🎯
description: Float32, float16, mixed precision, and how to cast between types.

slides.title: TensorFlow Data Types 📋
slides.content:
# Common dtypes
- `tf.float32` (default float)
- `tf.float16` (half precision, faster on GPUs)
- `tf.int32`, `tf.int64`
- `tf.bool`
- `tf.string`

> Analogy: Choosing the right measuring cup – ml vs. liters.

slides.title: Checking & Setting dtypes
slides.codeSnippet:
import tensorflow as tf

f = tf.constant(3.14)
print(f.dtype)  # tf.float32

i = tf.constant(42, dtype=tf.int64)
print(i.dtype)  # tf.int64

b = tf.constant(True)  # tf.bool

quizData.question: What is the default integer dtype in TensorFlow?
quizData.explanation: TensorFlow defaults to `int32` for integers and `float32` for floats.

slides.title: Casting Between Types 🔀
slides.content:
# `tf.cast(tensor, dtype)`

Convert a tensor to a different data type.

```python
a = tf.constant([1.7, 2.3])
b = tf.cast(a, tf.int32)   # truncates: [1,2]
c = tf.cast([0,1], tf.bool) # [False, True]
```

**Warning**: Casting float to int truncates, does not round.

quizData.question: After `tf.cast([2.9], tf.int32)`, what is the result?
quizData.explanation: Casting to int truncates the decimal, not rounds.

slides.title: Mixed Precision Training 🏎️
slides.content:
# Faster Training with float16

Modern GPUs have special hardware for `float16`. Mixed precision keeps some computations in `float32` for stability, others in `float16` for speed.

```python
from tensorflow.keras.mixed_precision import set_global_policy
set_global_policy('mixed_float16')
```

Layers automatically cast inputs to `float16`, outputs to `float32`.

slides.title: Precision Pitfalls ⚠️
slides.content:
## Underflow & Overflow

`float16` range is limited (~5.96e‑8 to 65504). Gradients can easily overflow or underflow. Use loss scaling in mixed precision.
